2. Methods
2.1. Animals and ethical approval
The experiments on mice in this study adhered to the animal protection regulations specified by German federal law and the standards of the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care. These experiments received approval and oversight from the local veterinary authority. The mice were housed in the animal facility at the Institute of Clinical Neurobiology, University Hospital of Wuerzburg, under controlled conditions. C57BL/6 mice, Nav1.8cre::CAGeGFP, and Na
V
1.9 knockout mice were kept on a 12-hour day/night cycle at temperatures between 20 and 22°C and humidity levels of 55% to 65%, with adequate food and water provided. Postnatal day 28 (P28) mice were used for all experiments. Randomization was not applied as the samples of different experimental conditions were processed in parallel to minimize technical variability. The experimental unit was the individual animal. No formal group assignment or treatment conditions were applied. Numbers per group are reported for each experiment. All mice were of C57BL/6 background, and animal experiments are reported per the ARRIVE 2.0 guidelines.
2.2. Skin punch biopsy collection
We obtained 6-mm skin punch biopsies from the right lateral lower leg of n = 4 healthy subjects (4 women) according to a standardized procedure.
73
Biopsies were performed under sterile conditions and after local anesthesia (1 mL, 10 mg/mL Mecain, Puren Pharma GmbH, Munich, Germany). A commercial punch device was used (Kai Medical, Seki, Japan). Skin samples were collected in 8°C cold, sterile, DMEM/F-12 medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, 11320-074). Afterwards, the epidermis was manually isolated from each biopsy sample with a scalpel and directly transferred into ice-cold homogenisation buffer (4 mM HEPES, 0.32 M Sucrose), 1× Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 78430), 40 U/mL RNAsin (Promega, Madison, WI) for further processing. Our study was approved by the Würzburg Medical School Ethics Committee (#49/23).
2.3. Peripheral nerve isolation from mouse footpads and human epidermis
The skin from mouse footpads or human biopsies was transferred into an ice-cold homogenization buffer (4 mM HEPES, 0.32 M Sucrose, 1× Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Scientific, 78430), 40 U/mL RNAsin (Promega, N2515). A glass tissue homogeniser was used with 12 gentle up-down strokes in 1:8 (wt/vol) of ice-cold homogenisation buffer. The total homogenate was centrifuged at 1000g for 10 minutes at 4°C (Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany, 5417R). The supernatant (S1) is removed carefully from the pellet (P1) and centrifuged at 14,600 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C. The supernatant (S2) is removed completely, and the resulting fraction is referred to as the peripheral nerve fraction. The same procedure was applied to human epidermal tissues. Aliquots of all fractions were stored at −80°C until further use.
2.4. Immunohistochemistry
The skin from the hind paw of P28 mice was dissected and fixed in 4% paraformaldeyde (PFA) for 2 hours at room temperature. The postfixed skin was embedded in 6% agarose in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Transverse sections of 40 µm were made using a vibratome (Leica VT1000S, Wetzlar, Germany). About 10 to 15 sections were collected and blocked in 10% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in PBS for 30 minutes at room temperature. For primary antibody labelling, the sections were incubated in antibodies for 48 hours at 4°C in a blocking solution containing 0.1% saponin and 1% BSA in PBS and immunolabeled with rabbit anti-PGP9.5 (1:10,000; Proteintech, Rosemont, IL, USA, 14730-1-AP), guinea pig anti-Syp1 (1:1000; SYSY, Goettingen, Germany, 101 308), mouse anti-Psd95 (1:1000; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 7E3-1B8), and chicken anti-GFP (1:5000; Abcam, Cambridge, United Kingdom, ab13970). The sections were washed 3 times with PBS for 5 minutes each. The sections were stained with secondary antibodies, donkey anti-rabbit Alexa488 (Jackson ImmunoResearch, West Grove, PA, 711-035-152), donkey anti-guinea pig Cy5 (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 706-175-148), donkey anti-mouse Cy3 (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 715-165-150), and donkey anti-chicken 488 (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 703-545-155) for 1 hour at room temperature and washed 4 times with PBS. The sections were stained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI; Sigma-Aldrich, Burlington, MA, D9542) for 5 minutes, washed 2 times with PBS and mounted on the objective slides, and embedded in FluorSave Reagent (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany, 345789).
2.5. Immunocytochemistry of peripheral nerve terminals
For peripheral nerve terminals antibody labelling, the protocol from Revelo et al.
57
was followed with a few modifications. The peripheral nerve terminals from n = 3 male mice per group were immobilised on 4 coverslips per mouse. The coverslips were precoated with 5% BSA. For fixation, 4% PFA in PBS was used and incubated at 4°C for 15 minutes on ice and 45 minutes at room temperature. Then, the peripheral nerve terminals were washed with PBS and quenched with 100 mM NH
4
Cl for 30 minutes. Peripheral nerve terminals were permeabilised and blocked using 0.1% Triton X-100 and 5% BSA in PBS. For primary antibody labelling, the peripheral nerve terminals were incubated in antibodies overnight at 4°C in a blocking solution. Then, the peripheral nerve terminals were washed 3 times with PBS and stained with secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature and washed 3 times with PBS. The following primary and secondary antibodies were used: chicken anti-Nefh (1:5000; EMD Millipore, Burlington, MA, USA, AB5539), mouse anti-Syn1 (1:1000; SYSY, 106 011), rabbit anti-Psd95 (1:1000; Abcam, ab18258), rabbit anti-Rpl24 (1:1000; Thermo Fisher Scientific, PA5-30157), mouse anti-Rps6 (1:100; Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA5-15123), mouse anti-Syp1 (1:1000; SYSY, 101 011), mouse anti-Tomm20 (1:100; Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA, SC-17764), donkey anti-chicken Alexa488 (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 703-545-155), donkey anti-mouse Cy3 (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 715-165-150), and donkey anti-rabbit Cy5 (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 711-175-152). Then, the coverslips were mounted on the objective slides and embedded in FluorSave Reagent (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany, 345789). The samples were imaged with an Olympus Fluoview 1000 confocal microscope.

The peripheral nerve terminals of n = 3 male mice per group were incubated with 0.1 µM of mCLING-ATTO 647N-labeled (Synaptic Systems, Goettingen, Germany, 710 006AT1) for 10 minutes at room temperature. Then, a pulse of 70 mM KCl for 5 minutes was applied. The peripheral nerve terminals were immobilised on 4 coverslips per mouse and then fixed with 4% PFA and 0.2% glutaraldehyde in PBS for 15 minutes on ice and 45 minutes at room temperature. Then, the peripheral nerve terminals were washed with PBS and quenched with 100 mM glycine in PBS for 5 minutes and 0.75 mM bromophenol blue for 5 minutes, and washed 3 times with PBS. Then, the coverslips were mounted on the objective slides and embedded in FluorSave Reagent. The samples were imaged with an Olympus Fluoview 1000 confocal microscope.

2
at room temperature). The skin was washed with 50 mM cacodylate buffer 3 times, 10 minutes each.

2.9. Super resolution array tomography sample preparation and immunolabelling
The skin from the hind paw of n = 2 male mice was dissected and fixed in 4% PFA for 2 hours at room temperature and further processed as detailed in Peters et al.

The sections were stained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI, Sigma-Aldrich, Burlington, MA, USA, D9542) for 5 minutes and washed 2 times, 2 minutes each with PBS and then with ddH
2
O. The slides were then dried, mounted with Mowiol 4 to 88 (Roth, Karlsruhe, Germany) and high-precision cover glass No. 1.5 H (Roth). Image acquisition was done using the Zeiss ELYRA S.1 SR-SIM system, equipped with a 63× oil-immersion Plan-Apochromat objective (NA 1.4 Oil Dic M27) and controlled by ZEN (Black Edition) software (all from Zeiss). A PCO Edge 5.5 sCMOS camera was used, with 3 rotations. Fluorescence images were processed using ImageJ (version 1.51n, NIH, Bethesda, MD), and channel alignment was done using Tetra speck beads (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, USA, PS-Speck Microscope Point Source Kit).
2.10. Electron microscopy sample preparation and imaging
For sample contrasting and carbon coating, cover glasses were removed, and Mowiol was washed out with ddH
2
O before being blow-dried. The glass area containing the ribbon was cut out using a diamond pen (Roth). Sections were then stained by applying a 2.5% (wt/vol) uranyl acetate solution (Merck) in ethanol for 15 minutes at room temperature. Afterward, sections underwent brief washes in 100% ethanol, 50% (vol/vol) ethanol in ddH
2
O, and 100% ddH
2
O. This was followed by a 10-minute incubation at room temperature in a 50% (vol/vol) lead citrate solution, prepared in decocted H
2
O with 80 mM of lead citrate (Merck), and 0.12 M of trisodium citrate (AppliChem). After rinsing with ddH
2
O, sections were dried and mounted onto specimen pin mounts using carbon conductive tape (Plano, Wetzlar, Germany). Conductive silver (Plano) was applied to establish electrical continuity between the glass and the holder edges. About 5-nm carbon coating was deposited using a CCU-010 carbon coating machine (Safematic, Bad Ragaz, Switzerland). Serial sections were imaged using a JSM-7500F field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM; JEOL) with an acceleration voltage of 5 kV. At each region of interest (ROI), multiple images were acquired at increasing magnifications.
2.11. Super resolution array tomography image processing and correlation
Montage and alignment of SEM images were performed using the ImageJ plugin TrakEM2.
9
Images of the same section taken at different magnifications were merged into a single layer using least squares montage in similarity mode, with an alignment error ranging from 10 to 20 pixels. Once each z-layer was positioned, serial 100-nm sections were aligned using the “align layers” function with similarity transformation mode and an alignment error of 20 pixels. The ROI from each layer was exported in TIF format.
To correlate immunofluorescence (IF) and SEM data, corresponding IF channel images and montaged SEM images were loaded into the vector graphics editor Inkscape (version 0.92.3) and processed following a standardized protocol.
41
,
42
Immunofluorescence channel images were overlaid and linked, with only the DAPI channel initially visible as a reference. The opacity of IF images was reduced to around 40%, and DAPI-labeled heterochromatin was used as an unbiased landmark for correlation and linked IF images were linearly transformed (rotated and resized without distortion) to match the orientation of cell nuclei in the EM images. Once an appropriate overlay was achieved, a rectangular area containing the ROI was extracted, and each layer was exported as a PNG file. Serial 100-nm sections were imaged via IF and correlated with their corresponding EM images.
2.12. Sample preparation for mass spectrometry
Samples subjected to quantitative mass spectrometry analysis were first alkylated and reduced using 10 mM Tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP), 40 mM of 2-chloracetamide (CAA) and 100 mM Tris-HCL (pH 8.5) in 1% (wt/vol) sodium deoxycholate (SDC) at 45°C for 5 minutes. Digestion was then done with a 1:1000 protein to LysC and trypsin (1:1) ratio overnight with 1400 rpm agitation on an Eppendorf Thermomixer C at 37°C. For desalting, peptides were first diluted tenfold using 1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) in isopropanol and loaded on SDB-RPS (Empore) StageTips.
56
The flowthrough was discarded, and StageTips were washed once with 200 mL of 1% TFA in isopropanol and then twice with 0.2% TFA/2% acetonitrile (ACN). Peptides were finally eluted using 60 mL of 80% ACN/1.25% NH
4
OH and dried using a SpeedVaccentrifuge (ConcentratorPlus; Eppendorf) for 1 hour at 30°C. Peptides were then resuspended in 0.2% TFA/2% ACN. Peptides of 200 ng were used for liquid chromatography-mass spectometry/mass spectometry analysis.
2.13. Data-independent acquisition
For the data-independent acquisition (DIA), we used the following mass spectrometry (MS) setup: 50 cm reversed-phase column (75 µm inner diameter, packed in-house with Reprosil-Pur C18-AQ 1.9 µm resin) that was kept at 50°C using a homemade column oven. The mass spectrometer (Orbitrap Exploris 480, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was connected online with an EASY-nLC 1200 system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For peptide separation, we used a binary buffer system consisting of 0.1% formic acid (FA) (buffer A) and 80% ACN, 0.1% FA (buffer B). We used a constant flow rate of 300 nL/minute and a 75-minute gradient. The gradient starts with 2% buffer B and gradually increases to 35% within 60 minutes, 60% within 70 minutes, and 90% within 71 minutes, and stays constant until 75 minutes. We used the following MS settings: data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode with a full scan range of 300 to 1650 m/z at resolution of 120,000, a maximum injection time of 20 milliseconds, automatic gain control of 3e6, with a stepped higher-energy collision dissociation (HCD) (set to 25, 27.5, and 30). After each full scan, 44 DIA scans were followed with a 30,000 resolution, an AGC of 1e6, and a maximum injection time of 54 milliseconds.
64
2.14. Data-independent acquisition data processing and data analysis
Data-independent acquisition by neural networks DIA-NN
14
1.8.1 was used as a search engine to process DIA raw files. Mus musculus and a human reference proteome with canonical and isoform sequences were used as the FASTA file, a text-based format for storing amino acid or nucleotide sequences. For the search, default settings were used with the following exceptions: for protein modification, we included carbamidomethylation, oxidation of methionine, and N-terminal acetylation. FASTA digest for library-free search and the deep learning–based spectra, RTs, and IMs predictions, including the heuristic protein inference, was turned on. Data analysis and visualization were done using Python v3.5.5 with the following libraries: seaborn 0.11.2, pandas 1.4.2, scikit-learn 1.5, numpy 1.21.5, matplotlib 3.5.13, statsmodels 0.13.5, and gseapy 1.0.4. Protein intensities were first log2 transformed to approximate a normal distribution. Data were then filtered for valid values in at least 1 experimental group. Imputation was done using a sampling method from a shifted Gaussian distribution with a shift of 3 and width of 0.3 standard deviations. Hierarchical clustering was performed using the Euclidean distance. For comparison of the S2 with the P1 fractions, n = 4 wild type mice or n = 4 human (women) biopsies were used. For comparison of the S2 fraction from wild type and Na
V
1.9 knockout (KO), quadruplicates were analysed, and 1 outlier was removed. Each group consisted of 3 males and 1 female. The data for the female mice were identified as outliers based on Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and, therefore, removed from the analysis. For determining statistical significance, we used an unpaired 2-tailed Student
t
-test. To address false positives, we adjusted the
P
-values using the Benjamini–Hochberg method. Enrichment analysis was done using the GSEAPY tool.
23
2.15. Search tool for the retrieval of interacting genes/proteins analysis
Differentially expressed proteins used for Search tool for the retrieval of interacting genes/proteins (STRING) analysis were defined as proteins exhibiting a log2 fold change ≥ 1 or ≤ −1 and a q-value < 0.05. Interactions with a STRING confidence score ≥ 0.7 were considered high confidence and retained for further analysis. Disconnected nodes in the network were removed, and the largest connected component was subjected to further analysis. Gene clusters enriched in specific biological processes, molecular functions, and cellular components were identified. Expression data were mapped on a network to visualise the upregulation or downregulation of cluster genes.
2.16. Image acquisition and data analysis
Images were acquired using an Olympus Fluoview 1000 confocal system equipped with the following objectives: 10× (NA: 0.25), 20× (NA: 0.75), 40× (oil differential interference contrast, NA: 1.30), and 60× (oil differential interference contrast, NA: 1.35). Fluorescence excitation was achieved with 405, 473, 559, and 633 nm lasers. Visualisation was done using the Olympus FV10-ASW (RRID: SCR_014215) imaging software. Structured illumination microscopy (SIM) was conducted with a commercial Zeiss Elyra S.1 microscope, featuring a Plan-Apochromat 63× NA 1.40 immersion oil–based objective and 4 excitation lasers: a 405 nm diode (50 mW), a 488 nm OPSL (100 mW), a 561 nm OPSL (100 mW), and a 642 nm diode laser (150 mW). The resulting images were processed by maximum intensity projection and adjusted for brightness and contrast using Image J software.
2.17. Statistics and reproducibility
All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 9 for Windows (GraphPad Software Inc., La Jolla, CA), and statistical significance was considered at
P
< 0.05. Quantitative data are presented as mean ± SD unless otherwise indicated. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. Blinding was not performed during group allocation, experimentation, or outcome assessment. No data were excluded from the analysis. For proteomics analysis, the female sample was removed from each group as an outlier based on MAD and PCA. After testing for normal distribution using the Shapiro–Wilk test, the data were subjected to further statistical analysis. Two groups were compared using unpaired 2-tailed Student
t
-tests or 2-tailed one-sample
t
-tests. For multiple independent groups, 1-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with post hoc multiple comparisons test was used. Details of replicate numbers, quantification, and statistics for each experiment are specified in the Figure legends.

1. Introduction
Chronic pain, a debilitating condition affecting millions worldwide, comprises both persistent and recurrent pain sensations that last beyond the expected time for tissue healing, often leading to profound physical and psychological distress.
40
,
45
The transition from acute to chronic pain involves a complex interplay of neurobiological processes in nociceptive sensory neurons located in dorsal root ganglia (DRG), including hyperexcitability of nociceptors, alterations in neuropeptide production and release, dysregulation of inflammatory mediators, and aberrant associations of nociceptive nerve terminals with the microenvironment in affected areas.
39
,
61
While pain-signalling mechanisms have been shown to alter gene expression and protein production in somas of DRG sensory neurons, and also synaptic transmission in the spinal cord,
3
,
12
,
13
much less is known about cutaneous proteome alterations occurring in peripheral nerve terminals in the context of pain.
The peripheral branches of cutaneous DRG sensory neurons innervate the epidermis and dermis
62
where they are in contact with multiple cell types. Nociceptive signalling is influenced locally by such non-neuronal cells like macrophages, immune cells, nociceptive Schwann cells, and keratinocytes, which play an important role in modulating pain thresholds and sensitivity within the emerging concept of cutaneous nociception.
34
,
58
Keratinocytes are the predominant cells in the epidermis and are involved in direct communication with the peripheral sensory nerve forming the neurocutaneous unit.
22
,
70
They are also involved in signal transduction and nociception.
4
,
66
,
69
In this study, we isolated peripheral nerve terminals from the mouse footpad by developing a protocol based on techniques that were previously applied for synaptosome isolation from the central nervous system.
6
We observed the presence of several pre- and postsynaptic proteins in isolated nerve terminals and performed mass spectrometry to identify the proteome of these terminals. Further, we analysed nerve terminals of Na
V
1.9 knockout mice, which show impaired mechanical and thermal sensory capacities along with diminished electrical excitability of nociceptors.
29
This identified translation and mitochondrial energy metabolism as well as signalling cascades such as the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and extracellular regulated kinase 1/2 (ERK1/2), which appear particularly relevant for pain perception. In addition, the isolation of human nerve terminals from skin punch biopsies, as validated by proteomic analysis, underscores the extensive and translational significance of our approach. Therefore, our data reveal the proteomic diversity of peripheral nerve terminals, and the techniques outlined here could be applied to study local protein alterations in models of chronic pain, pain resolution as well as in diagnostic human biomaterial.

2.13. Data-independent acquisition
For the data-independent acquisition (DIA), we used the following mass spectrometry (MS) setup: 50 cm reversed-phase column (75 µm inner diameter, packed in-house with Reprosil-Pur C18-AQ 1.9 µm resin) that was kept at 50°C using a homemade column oven. The mass spectrometer (Orbitrap Exploris 480, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was connected online with an EASY-nLC 1200 system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For peptide separation, we used a binary buffer system consisting of 0.1% formic acid (FA) (buffer A) and 80% ACN, 0.1% FA (buffer B). We used a constant flow rate of 300 nL/minute and a 75-minute gradient. The gradient starts with 2% buffer B and gradually increases to 35% within 60 minutes, 60% within 70 minutes, and 90% within 71 minutes, and stays constant until 75 minutes. We used the following MS settings: data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode with a full scan range of 300 to 1650 m/z at resolution of 120,000, a maximum injection time of 20 milliseconds, automatic gain control of 3e6, with a stepped higher-energy collision dissociation (HCD) (set to 25, 27.5, and 30). After each full scan, 44 DIA scans were followed with a 30,000 resolution, an AGC of 1e6, and a maximum injection time of 54 milliseconds.

3.2. Isolated peripheral nerve terminals contain active protein translational machinery
To characterise the isolated peripheral nerve terminals, we immobilised them on coverslips following a method previously introduced by Ramirez et al.

4

36
,
65

4

To evaluate the functionality of peripheral nerve terminals, we incubated the S2 fraction with the membrane labelling dye mCLING, which can be used to monitor membrane trafficking. This dye can be used to measure the dynamics of synaptic and other types of exocytosed vesicles, because it binds to the plasma membrane of these structures

Stimulation of peripheral nerve terminals with KCl at room temperature induced mCLING uptake in 76.2% of nerve endings, compared to only 19.1% in the absence of KCl, which may be attributed to passive diffusion at room temperature (Figs.
4

4. Discussion
Chronic pain is an incapacitating disorder representing a substantial health burden, affecting 1 in 5 people in Europe, and for half of these individuals, treatment is inadequate.
7
,
20
While previous studies describe mechanisms underlying gene expression and protein translation alterations in sensory neurons during chronic pain,
53
considerably less is understood about local proteome alterations in peripheral nerve endings at the neurocutaneous unit. The approach proposed here uses the isolation of peripheral nerve terminals from mouse footpads that are densely innervated with nociceptor terminals.
The skin is innervated by a heterogeneous population of sensory afferents, including both nociceptive and non-nociceptive fibers, as well as autonomic fibers.
8
,
18
,
26
While our study primarily focuses on nociceptive afferents, we acknowledge that non-nociceptive sensory fibers, such as mechanoreceptors, which are primarily located in the dermis and, in some cases, extend into the epidermis. Proprioceptors, in contrast, are not typically found in the skin but are in muscles, tendons, and joints. In addition, autonomic fibers are present in the dermis, where they innervate structures such as blood vessels, sweat glands, and arrector pili muscles. Although our protocol for biochemical isolation of nerve terminals does not specifically differentiate between sensory and autonomic fibers, we provide evidence for the presence of synaptic components in nociceptive nerve endings. The immunohistochemistry results illustrated an overlap between pre- and postsynaptic markers with PGP9.5 in footpad sections of wild type mice and with GFP in footpad sections from Na
V
1.8cre::CAGeGFP mice, which was confirmed by the presence of synaptic markers and PGP9.5 in the S2 fraction after fractionation. The observation of GFP in the S2 fraction from Na
V
1.8cre::CAGeGFP footpads provides evidence for the enrichment nociceptor terminals with the isolation method described here. Interestingly, the electron micrograph of the skin suggests the presence of close contact sites between the peripheral nerve and keratinocytes.
70
While we detected presynaptic vesicle components (Syp) in close proximity to the postsynaptic marker Psd95 at these sites, we did not find evidence of classical synapses, such as pronounced membrane specializations like pre- and postsynaptic thickenings. This lack of classical morphology suggests that these contacts may represent transient
en passant
-like synaptic contacts with keratinocytes in the epidermis, as previously reported by others.
68
,
70
One of the most relevant findings of our study is the detection of both pre- and postsynaptic structures in the S2 fraction. This result indicates the presence of synapse-like contacts between sensory nerve terminals and epidermal cells, most likely keratinocytes. Signalling from keratinocytes to nociceptors has been shown before,
4
indicating a modulatory function of skin cells for pain perception. More recently, contacts between keratinocytes and sensory afferents have also been observed at the ultrastructural level.
22
In line with previous studies,
37
,
43
we also detected components of the translational machinery and mitochondrial proteins in nerve terminals, underscoring their capacity for energy metabolism
19
and protein synthesis. This agrees with several studies that have identified an enrichment of mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins, translation-associated proteins (translation initiation and elongation factors), and components of the cytoskeleton in neurites.
46
,
76
While the significance of this enrichment is currently not completely understood, the presence and local synthesis of components of the translation machinery might reflect the need for protein production in nerve terminals during stimulation or plasticity. In addition, ribosomes might undergo local remodeling in axons and nerve terminals in the context of such plasticity processes.
25
,
60
In line with these observations, ribosomes are not only present in the cell body but have also been detected in the terminals of sensory neurons.
78
Importantly, the S2 fraction is also depleted of histone and keratin proteins for both mice and human skin samples, which further indicates the efficiency of the enrichment procedure.
Na
V
1.9 plays an important role in the induction of thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity, both in subacute and chronic inflammatory pain models. Hence, we applied an unbiased proteomics approach to identify proteins enriched in wild type relative to Na
V
1.9 KO terminals, as these proteins indicate pathways required for pain perception. Interestingly, we observed components of the ERK1/2 and MAPK signalling pathways upregulated in wild type terminals. These pathways are activated during pain in an NGF-dependent fashion. NGF has been demonstrated to increase the expression of the heat-sensitive transient receptor potential (TRP) channel, TRPV1, via activation of the tyrosine kinase receptor (Trk) A/p38 MAPK pathway.
35
In addition, we observed increased levels of Nefl in wild type relative to Na
V
1.9 KO nerve terminals. Elevated levels of Nefl have been detected in peripheral serum in patients with bortezomib-induced polyneuropathy,
10
and these elevated levels might not only reflect enhanced release from degenerating neurons but also increased production in sensory neurons with augmented pain perception.
We successfully adapted our peripheral nerve isolation technique to extract and analyse human nerve terminal proteins from diagnostic skin punch biopsy samples. In the context of hardly available human sensory neuron and nerve biomaterial for research and diagnostics, we present an innovative, minimally invasive approach, to directly investigate nociceptors on molecular level at the neurocutaneous unit, which may have major implications for differential diagnostics and for the determination of potential therapeutic targets for analgesic and neuroprotective treatment approaches.
In conclusion, we optimised a method initially used for the isolation of synaptosomes from CNS to obtain isolated nerve endings from the mouse footpad skin. The method was further validated by a translational approach on human skin punch biopsies. We applied this method to the well-studied Na
V
1.9 KO mouse model and identified pathways important for nociception. This strategy can be further translated into both mouse pain models and human pain syndromes and help to understand the local proteomic and transcriptomic alterations in peripheral nerve branches associated with pain development, chronification, and resolution.
